questions.stem: Leticia, 35, has returned from India 3 weeks ago with fever, RUQ ache, dark urine and pale stools. You are in the ED examining her abdomen and want to find the edge of a possibly enlarged, tender liver. How should you palpate for the liver edge?
options: Start just below the right costal margin and press deeply as she breathes out
Start in the epigastrium and move laterally along the costal margin as she breathes out
Start in the right iliac fossa and move up towards the costal margin as she breathes in
Start in the left upper quadrant and sweep across to the right as she breathes in
questions.why: Start low in the right iliac fossa so you do not miss a large liver. Then advance your hand towards the costal margin a little with each breath, feeling for the edge to hit your fingers as the diaphragm pushes the liver down on inspiration.
notes: If you start at the costal margin, your hand can already be over a large liver and you will miss its edge. The liver also comes down on inspiration, not expiration.
The liver moves down on inspiration, so palpating as she breathes out works against you. Starting in the epigastrium also misses a liver edge lying low in the right flank.
This is the route for the spleen, which enlarges from the left upper quadrant towards the right iliac fossa. It is not how you look for the liver edge.

questions.stem: Leticia, 35, was in rural India with no malaria prophylaxis and few mosquito nets. Her temperature is 38.1 °C. Hepatitis A IgM is detected. Her first malaria antigen test and thick and thin films are negative. Platelets are normal. What should be done next about malaria?
options: No further testing, as the confirmed hepatitis A explains her fever
Repeat thick and thin films with antigen 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 sets are negative
Start empirical artemether-lumefantrine now and repeat films only if she remains febrile
Send malaria serology at her 2-week follow-up appointment
questions.why: One negative set does not exclude malaria in a febrile traveller. Repeat films and antigen testing 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 sets are negative, even when another diagnosis has been confirmed.
notes: Having one diagnosis does not rule out another. She has unprotected exposure in an area with P. falciparum and P. vivax, and a single negative set is not enough.
Antimalarials are given for a confirmed diagnosis. Empirical treatment is only for severe illness when testing is unavailable, and she is stable with tests under way.
Serology shows past exposure, not current infection, and waiting 2 weeks could miss falciparum malaria, which can kill within days.

questions.stem: Leticia, 35, has acute hepatitis A with ALT 2840 U/L. Her INR is 1.1 and albumin 39 g/L. The registrar says the INR, not the albumin, is the result to watch for early liver failure. What is the main physiological reason?
options: Albumin is lost in the vomitus, so its level reflects losses rather than synthesis
The INR measures how bilirubin impairs platelet function in hepatitis
Albumin falls only once fibrosis develops, so it stays normal for weeks in acute illness
Factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours, so the INR rises within a day of failure
questions.why: The liver makes the clotting factors, and factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours, so the INR rises quickly when synthesis fails. Albumin's half-life is about 3 weeks, so it stays normal early. Judge severity by INR, glucose and mental state.
notes: Vomitus contains very little protein, so vomiting does not lower serum albumin to any useful degree.
The INR is a measure of the prothrombin time, which reflects clotting factor activity. It has nothing to do with platelet function.
Albumin can fall in acute illness too, but slowly because of its long half-life. The issue is timing, not whether fibrosis is present.

questions.stem: Leticia, 35, has fever and right upper quadrant pain after travel, and cholecystitis is on your differential. You test for Murphy's sign by pressing over the gallbladder fundus while she breathes in. Where is the surface marking of the gallbladder fundus?
options: Tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, at the lateral edge of rectus
Tip of the right 11th rib in the midaxillary line, below the lower costal margin
In the midline just below the xiphisternum
Right renal angle, below the 12th rib posteriorly
questions.why: The gallbladder fundus lies at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the linea semilunaris (lateral edge of rectus abdominis) meets the costal margin. If she stops breathing in when you press there, Murphy's sign is positive.
notes: The 11th rib tip in the midaxillary line overlies the lateral liver and hepatic flexure, too far lateral and posterior for the gallbladder fundus.
The area below the xiphisternum is the epigastrium, overlying the stomach and left lobe of the liver. Tenderness here suggests peptic disease or pancreatitis.
The renal angle is where you check for kidney tenderness, as in pyelonephritis. The gallbladder lies in front, not at the back.
